title: AI Is Dead. Organoids Are Alive
excerpt: Mini human brains are being grown in labs all over the world. Soon, they could outthink neural networks.
content_html:
I’m going to let you in on a secret. Every cell in your body has the potential to get smarter. I don’t mean this metaphorically, or in a “body keeps the score” kind of way. I mean that if lab-coated biologists took a sample of your skin and very carefully manipulated the cells inside it, they could actually make a brain. They do it all the time.

Not a brain as complex as the one behind your eyes, of course, but a glob of gray matter nonetheless, with a few-million-odd neurons that can send and receive electrical signals. Biologists call these strange creations human brain organoids. Kept at a womblike 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit for eight months, they’ll produce repetitive oscillations—brain waves—nearly indistinguishable from those made by a premature baby.

In cell culture labs around the world, human brain organoids live out their short lives as neural guinea pigs, testing the effects of diseases, toxins, and new pharmaceuticals. But they may soon be on to more glamorous pursuits. At the University of San Diego, organoids are guiding spidery robots through mazes and taking hero doses of psychedelics. At Johns Hopkins, they’re forming the basis of novel biocomputing systems. And at a startup in Melbourne, they’re playing video games like Pong and Doom.

Biologists do the darnedest things. While the rest of us are distracted by large language models and AI agents, they’re going straight to the source of intelligence, cultivating living neurons and teaching themselves to program them with electrical signals and hits of dopamine. In the future, they wager, artificial intelligence won’t be artificial at all. It’ll be built from the stuff of life itself.

The most metal building at UC San Diego is the library. An inverted concrete ziggurat, the Geisel Library—named for the children’s author better known as Dr. Seuss—looms over an otherwise bucolic campus on spindly, two-story legs. On a recent afternoon, as a marine layer hung low in the eucalyptus groves, it looked particularly like the mothership of a brutalist alien race.

That day, the Geisel’s sunken lobby was hung with scientific images from the university’s collection. Among CGI renderings of folded proteins and macrophotographs of benthic sea creatures, one image stuck out. It depicted a clump of human brain cells, silhouetted in black against the milky white of a petri dish. A corona of axons, the threadlike nerve endings that transmit electrical impulses across the brain, stretched outward from the clump with palpable yearning.

Whether in our skulls or in a dish, neurons want nothing more than to find one another—and, across the emptiness, to forge the synapses whose electrical chattering forms the basis of thought. They’re very good at it. If you put loose brain cells together, they will multiply and interlink until they’ve cohered into autonomous globs of tissue. Human brain organoids practically make themselves.

A 20-minute walk from the Geisel, at UCSD’s Sanford Stem Cell Institute, they’re making themselves in the tens of thousands. “Whatever environment you put them in, the first thing that they do is try to connect,” said the Brazilian developmental biologist Alysson Muotri, as we gazed over the blue plane of Pacific outside his office window. “Connect with the dishes, connect with the electrodes, connect to each other. This is an intrinsic property of our brain, to connect.”

Muotri is dashing, with a surfer’s tan and the aquiline profile of a figure on an ancient Roman coin. Over the past decade, his lab has dramatically expanded the scope of brain organoid research. He and his colleagues have revived genetic material from the hominin fossil record to create “Neanderthalized” brain organoids. They have sent organoid payloads to the International Space Station to study what cosmic radiation does to astronaut brains. But the issue closest to Muotri’s heart is autism. His 18-year-old son is autistic and receives 24-hour care. By studying brain organoids grown from the cells of autistic donors—including his son—he hopes to pinpoint where the neural development of autistic children differs from their neurotypical counterparts.

This is not an invasive procedure. To make a brain organoid, all you need is that sample of skin I mentioned before. (Samples of blood, hair, or teeth work too.) You take the adult cells and introduce them to some special proteins that revert them to their embryonic state. Given a second chance to mature, these so-called induced pluripotent stem cells can become anything: tear gland organoids that cry, heart organoids that beat, or brain organoids that … well, that’s the question.

In utero brain development is, as one bioethicist told me, “a black box” of scientific knowledge. Historically, a lot of what we know about it is inferred from studies with mice. But with an organoid, the transformation of stem cells into neurons into brain tissue happens in full view. In theory, scientists could one day study how a colony of dividing cells comes together to create a mind—to make, from 86 billion neurons, a person named Alysson Muotri, for example.

Or another one named Claire L. Evans, who at this moment is leaning over Muotri’s shoulder to gape at a dish of floating brainlets under the microscope. Visually, organoids are not compelling; they’re opaque, snot-colored, the approximate size and shape of a chia seed. Muotri’s organoids contain 5 million cells, of which 2.5 million are neurons. (The rest are non-neural glial cells, which serve as scaffolding.) This, he reassures me, is the size of a bee’s brain. I suspect this is his way of tempering any ethical ick I may have. Although the evidence for insect sentience is growing, invertebrate research is still exempt from federal animal welfare laws. As John Evans, a sociologist and the codirector of UCSD’s Institute for Practical Ethics, put it to me when I wandered over to his office for the humanist take, “You don’t need to get permission to torture as many flies as you want.”

For now, you don’t need permission to torture brain organoids either. From a bioethical perspective, they aren’t people; they’re not even animals. If organoids someday graduate from bee to mouse size, this protocol would have to evolve. The trouble is, nobody knows quite where to draw a line. Sentience is hardly a settled idea; it’s not even clear you can have sentience without a body or a sensory experience of the world. And forget about calling an organoid conscious. “Imagine that you had spent your life in a glass tube—could you possibly even think of what you have as consciousness?” Evans asked me. “Philosophers of mind will tell you that what we call consciousness is not possible without experiences.” To make a conscious organoid, he added, “you first have to start having organoids have experiences.”

This isn’t impossible. We’ve all seen The Matrix. To the brain, the whole Ferris wheel of life is just pings of chemistry and electricity. To give an organoid an “experience,” all Muotri has to do is pluck one from its amniotic goo, place it on a conductive sheet of graphene, and—not to put too fine a point on it—zap it.

Do the organoids like being zapped? Muotri isn’t sure. What he does know is that they respond to electrical signals, remember them, and eventually come to anticipate them. For him, that’s evidence that they’re maturing, becoming more useful models of human development. But for other researchers, this electrical communication represents something else entirely: that living matter, like a computer, is programmable. And this is where things get truly weird.

It’s 3:30 pm in Los Angeles, which means it’s tomorrow morning in Australia. I’m sitting on the fire escape of my office building, peering at a grid of 59 squares on my laptop screen. I’ve been told that each of the squares represents an electrode in the Melbourne laboratory of the biocomputing startup Cortical Labs. And on each of those electrodes is a tiny culture of living human neurons. At the moment, my screen is registering fleeting spikes from those neurons—the spontaneous activity of brain matter in a vacuum. I click a square, zapping off an electrical hello to neurons 8,000 miles away. In response, all 59 electrodes spike at once.

For a moment, I’m giddy with a feeling of new power. I click around, sending those distant neurons hopping; my screen fills with the peaks and valleys of their electrical pulses. I page over to the neurons’ environmental settings. If I wanted to, I could drop their onboard temperature or nuke their precise gas mix of oxygen and CO2. If I did that, they’d certainly die. It’s about as significant a paradigm shift as I can imagine for computing: No matter how badly you mess up your code, things on the computer don’t normally die in real life.

But that’s the reality of the Cortical Cloud. In Melbourne, Cortical Labs cultivates flat neural cultures—the stem cells were donated by the company’s own founder—and loads them into sleek white biological “computers” called CL-1s. Each is the size of an elongated toaster and boasts an onboard life-support system capable of keeping a culture of up to a million neurons alive for six months. With the CL-1, Cortical Labs is aiming to become the Nvidia of neural computing, providing hardware and, let’s say, “neurons as a service” with a sub-millisecond delay.

For now, these neural computers are mostly of interest to researchers who want to work with neurons without taking on the tedious wet-lab husbandry themselves. Eventually, however, the company hopes that neurons will prove themselves to be an energy-efficient, resilient substrate for more general computing applications—including some tasks currently handled by AI, like image recognition and classification.

“When you think about what you want from AI, it’s biology,” said Brett Kagan, Cortical Labs’ chief operating officer, when I reached him over Zoom. “You want it to be self-repairing as much as possible. You want it to be adaptable. You want it to be long-lived. You want it to be energy-efficient. These are all features you get for free in biology.”

Kagan is a new father; as we spoke, his toddler ran riot in the background. But he’s no stranger to young and unruly forms of intelligence. In 2022, using a system similar to what currently powers the Cortical Cloud, Kagan grew a neural culture on a microchip and trained it to play the 1972 Atari game Pong, rewarding the neurons with predictable electrical pulses when they made correct decisions and punishing them with chaotic bursts when they made mistakes.

The technique served as a minimal proof of concept for a theory, proposed by the neuroscientist Karl Friston, that self-organizing biological systems tend to minimize surprise whenever possible. By showing that neurons will reorganize themselves to avoid chaotic stimulus, Cortical Labs demonstrated one possible approach for programming living matter. But the experiment also signaled that the CL-1 could be considered hardware for testing theories of cognition. “Not to try and make our stuff sound so grandiose,” Kagan told me, “but I would say the CL-1 is to theoretical neuroscience as the Large Hadron Collider was to theoretical physics.”

Kagan, to be fair, enjoys a grandiose claim. In the Pong paper, he and his colleagues claimed that the neurons, “embodied” within the game, displayed a form of sentience. Many in the research community balked at this cavalier use of language; one particularly polemic response, published in the journal Neuron, accused Cortical Labs of “hijacking” the very concept of sentience.

But as Alon Loeffler, a scientist at Cortical Labs, later explained to me, our brains are embedded in an environment, and responding to that environment in real time is what brains do—it’s what brains are for. Since neurons in a dish don’t benefit from those constant feedback loops of action and experience, the game fills the gap. “A game is just a version of the world,” Loeffler said.

The Pong program comes preinstalled on the Cortical Cloud, as a package of easily deployable Python code. When I ran the Australian neurons through a two-hour session, I watched as they incrementally improved their game in real time. In the end, their longest rally was 10 accurate shots, which beats my tennis game handily. It was impressive, but now the neurons are leveling up.

For one, they have learned to play Doom.

When I set out to report this story, I was sure it was about consciousness: the eerie moment a quarter-peanut of flesh sparks with self-knowledge, and what that precipice means for the researchers responsible. I imagined long dark nights of the cell and tiny funerals for spent neurons. What I found, however, was that nearly all scientists who keep organoids see the consciousness question as a distraction.

Most bristle when asked. They gesture to the organoids themselves—tiny balls bobbing in liquid solution like droplets of olive oil in vinegar—as if to say, give me a break. “Consciousness is so qualitative,” complained Annie Kathuria, an organoid researcher, when I visited her lab at Johns Hopkins. “How am I supposed to measure something qualitative on a tissue that’s floating in a dish? Someone has to define it. That’s what I say to everyone: Define to me what consciousness is, in quantitative terms.”

The request is rhetorical, of course. Humans have been trying to define consciousness since the days of Plato and nobody’s come close to nailing down the general idea, let alone a list of quantitative metrics. But it reflects a strong tendency in biology labs to want to focus on the practical, rather than the philosophical. When I spoke to Kathuria, she sipped from a Venti Starbucks tea and regularly glanced at the whiteboard over my shoulder, covered in a list of dozens of drug screenings her lab was on the hook for. Defining the nature of mind was the last thing on her mind.

That’s a job for the philosophers. Publishing papers about the edge cases of sentience has become something of a cottage industry in contemporary philosophy. Do zombies have moral status? Should robots have rights? What is it like to be a bat? Is an organoid sentient? Opinions vary. The philosopher Tim Bayne worries that organoids, isolated in their petri dishes, could become “islands of awareness.” Jonathan Birch, a professor of philosophy at the London School of Economics, thinks we’re in trouble if organoids ever grow a brain stem, which he argues functions as a “power cable” for consciousness.

Others suggest thresholds based on the number of neurons, or organoid size. But thresholds are difficult to quantify too. “You cannot draw a barrier that will hold based on a number,” explained John Evans, the sociologist at UCSD. “You could say ‘you can’t grow anything larger than 4 millimeters.’ Well, how about 5 millimeters? There’s no morally relevant distinction between the two.”

Conveniently, organoids can’t grow much bigger than 5 millimeters anyway. Once they reach a certain size, without a vascular system to pump in oxygen and pump out metabolic wastes, they develop a “necrotic core” and suffocate. This has created an upper ceiling for the organoid debate, but it won’t hold much longer. At Johns Hopkins, the nanotechnologist David Gracias is developing biomimetic artificial arteries; across town, at the Medical School, Kathuria creates rough blood vessel networks from endothelial organoids. Researchers are keeping organoids alive longer and longer. Muotri’s record, of three years, might’ve gone longer had someone in his lab not dropped the dish.

“The goal is to get to a 1-centimeter brain organoid,” said Thomas Hartung, as he walked me around the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing, or CAAT, at Johns Hopkins, where he’s experimenting with new perfusion systems to get around the bloodlessness problem. One centimeter is roughly the size of a mouse brain—“a completely different beast,” Hartung said, than the 500-micrometer organoids he’s accustomed to.

Hartung, a German-born toxicologist, has been working with organoids for over a decade. He’s the picture of a genial scientist. When we met, he sported an oversized cardigan and a beaded necklace made by his 9-year-old daughter. His wife, Lena Smirnova, is a neurotoxicologist and runs a lab at CAAT. Where Hartung is bearish and avuncular, with the loping Teutonic accent of a laid-back Werner Herzog, Smirnova is petite, with a bowl cut and a punctilious manner. The odd coupling seems to work for them. When I asked Smirnova if she’d ever make an organoid out of her own cells, she laughed so abruptly it sounded like she barked. “This is actually something between the two of us,” Hartung said, sheepishly. He’d offered her some of his stem cells, as an act of love, and she has so far refused to do anything with them.

Hartung and Smirnova are leading figures in organoid research and have been vocal public supporters of the idea that organoids will revolutionize computing. In 2023, after organizing an international scholarly community, they published a splashy “Declaration” for a field they christened “organoid intelligence,” or OI. During my visit, however, the organoids in the CAAT lab weren’t doing much computing. They were mostly being dosed with heavy metals. OI is a buzzy idea, and it has drawn a lot of media attention. But practically, it’s a long-term goal. For now, organoids remain what they have always been—glorified lab rats.

Nearly every organoid researcher I met reporting this piece told me the same fact: that in human clinical trials, the failure rate for neuropsychiatric drugs is close to 95 percent. The pipeline for new medications for conditions like depression, Alzheimer’s, and epilepsy is long, and often dry. That’s because drugs are ordinarily tested on animals, not people, and animal testing has never been the most physiologically relevant way to ensure the efficacy of drugs—it’s just been the most practical one. Organoids have changed that calculus.

“Think about nonhuman primates, which is the model closest to us—these monkeys with electrodes in their heads,” Hartung said. “At best, you have a battery of five, six monkeys sitting there and doing their experiments. We’re producing, in one six-well plate, up to 4,000 brain organoids.” In this context, OI isn’t an end as much as it is a means. An organoid trained to play Pong, for example, is a perfect test subject to study how drugs affect learning and memory.

In his office, Hartung showed me a simple video game his team is working on—a platformer with varying obstacles for the brain organoids to “jump” over. The idea is to train the organoids to respond to electrical signals representing those obstacles. Once they’ve learned this task, Hartung can ask questions like: How long do brain organoids remember when to “jump”? What effect do Alzheimer’s drugs have on the strength and duration of those memories?

Underneath his desk, Hartung keeps a cardboard box filled with bottles of red wine, which he suggested we crack open twice before I left. He believes all the best conversations happen after 5 pm, and he paid for his graduate studies, back in Germany, doing stand-up comedy (he compares his comedic style to Bill Maher’s). The years of gigging gave him a head for PR.

Organoid intelligence is, above all, good PR—a savvily branded attractor for funding and talent in a wide-open field. “I think the pie is too big for anybody to eat,” he said, leaning back in his chair. “What is really important is to tell the people about the opportunity of the pie so that we jointly have a feast. I will try as quickly as possible to eat my piece, which is the use for this in drug development, or in identifying substances which are impacting brain diseases. That’s my business.”

Business is booming. In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health announced that it will no longer award grant funding to research that relies exclusively on animal testing, encouraging consideration of “new approach models,” like organoids, instead; in September, the NIH announced an $87 million investment in building a Standardized Organoid Modeling Center. Fortunately for the NIH, since organoids are made with induced pluripotent stem cells from consenting adult donors, they don’t inspire the same religious ire as embryonic stem cell research did in the 1990s. And unlike lab rats or primates, organoid testing doesn’t irk the animal rights crowd.

Recent studies suggest that ordinary people, by and large, aren’t much bothered by organoids. When they do lodge an objection, it’s not because globs of neural cells might someday achieve human-level sentience. It’s because brain organoids are creepy. They muddy the line between person and thing, which, like the difference between humans and animals, or between the dead and the living, is a fundamental distinction that transcends cultures.

In 2017, a pair of neuroscientists at University College London took a small sample of skin cells from the science journalist Philip Ball’s arm and made them into a brain organoid. Eight months later, gazing at their creation under the microscope, Ball felt an “unsettling frisson” at the idea that this living tissue, formed from his flesh as Eve from Adam’s rib, pulsed with the same electrical signals that animated his own brain. Although their structure was comparatively primitive, the neurons in Ball’s organoid were nonetheless communicating with one another. “These are not ‘thoughts,’” he told himself. “But they are what thoughts are made from.”

Cajoled into becoming a mini-brain, Ball’s cells shifted ontological categories. Nobody could deny they were still alive, but it wasn’t Ball’s life they were living anymore. As Ball observes in his book How to Grow a Human, life is supposed to be a one-way journey: Sperm fertilizes egg, egg becomes zygote, and from this single cell cleave the trillions of facets that make us. This “seems conceptually unproblematic, so long as we can regard it all along as a coherent, boundaried organism with a unique history,” Ball writes. “But if you can take a tiny part of that mass of cells, rewind the tape and make a fresh start, then this unity starts to dissolve.” Kept warm and well fed in a petri dish, our cells carry on quite happily without us. Are they still ours?

Somewhere between the few million neurons in a brain organoid and the billions more that make up our minds, selfhood emerges—and absolutely nobody knows when. It reminds me of something the gnomic science-fiction writer Ted Chiang observed in a 2021 interview. “Suffering precedes moral agency in the developmental ladder,” he said. “In the process of developing machines that are conscious and moral agents, we will be inevitably creating billions of entities that are capable of suffering. And we will inevitably inflict suffering on them.”

Chiang was talking about AI, but his point stands. After all, as digital interfaces between neural wetware and silicon hardware improve, we’ll have a harder time differentiating between the two, and it’s reasonable to imagine that efforts to engineer and standardize biological intelligence will inform the design of future AI systems. But what struck me, as I visited one cell culture lab after another, is the way their values inverted, rather than mimicked, those of the AI business.

For the AI people, machine intelligence seems achievable, even inevitable. They “feel the AGI.” Part of this is hype; part of it is a willingness to take intelligence for what it does, as opposed to what it is. “If it quacks like a duck, it is a duck,” said John Evans, the UCSD sociologist. “The Silicon Valley types are super pragmatic. If AI is capable of doing what a human with consciousness does, they’ll call it consciousness.”

Biologists who work with neural cultures, however, are far less likely to use such a word without plenty of agonizing caveats. These biologists cultivate the raw meat of mind every day; they’re in the privileged position to understand how colossally complex it really is. As biology and AI converge, the culture shock between these worldviews is likely to be bracing.

For now, it seems that in the race toward conscious machines, there will be two lanes. One will be paved with rare earth minerals and silicon—forced, at enormous financial and energy cost, to model the brain from the top-down, in the form of artificial neural networks. Although there’s a lot these systems can do well, they will never be brains. Nothing forged from silicon ever could. As Cortical Labs’ Brett Kagan put it, “How can you have a truly adaptable, flexible system in an inflexible substrate?”

Which leaves the other path. Admittedly, this one will be slippery and meandering—adapting, as all living things do, to the journey as it goes. It might not be the most direct route, but in the evolutionary history of life on Earth, it’s the only thing that has ever led to intelligence.

So I’m betting on the neurons. I made up my mind back at that strange mothership of a library in San Diego, when I saw those axons reaching for one another across the void. Something in the innocence of their striving moved me. After all, my cells and yours have been doing the same thing since the day we were born. Trying to connect. And one thing we can count on—through the rise and fall of silicon—is that they’re never going to stop.

In Melbourne, Cortical Labs cultivates flat neural cultures—the stem cells were donated by the company’s own founder—and loads them into sleek white biological “computers” called CL-1s. Each is the size of an elongated toaster and boasts an onboard life-support system capable of keeping a culture of up to a million neurons alive for six months. With the CL-1, Cortical Labs is aiming to become the Nvidia of neural computing, providing hardware and, let’s say, “neurons as a service” with a sub-millisecond delay.For now, these neural computers are mostly of interest to researchers who want to work with neurons without taking on the tedious wet-lab husbandry themselves. Eventually, however, the company hopes that neurons will prove themselves to be an energy-efficient, resilient substrate for more general computing applications—including some tasks currently handled by AI, like image recognition and classification.“When you think about what you want from AI, it’s biology,” said Brett Kagan, Cortical Labs’ chief operating officer, when I reached him over Zoom. “You want it to be self-repairing as much as possible. You want it to be adaptable. You want it to be long-lived. You want it to be energy-efficient. These are all features you get for free in biology.”Brett Kagan, of Cortical Labs, believes his neural cultures display a form of sentience.PHOTOGRAPH COURTESY OF CORTICAL LABSKagan is a new father; as we spoke, his toddler ran riot in the background. But he’s no stranger to young and unruly forms of intelligence. In 2022, using a system similar to what currently powers the Cortical Cloud, Kagan grew a neural culture on a microchip and trained it to play the 1972 Atari game Pong, rewarding the neurons with predictable electrical pulses when they made correct decisions and punishing them with chaotic bursts when they made mistakes.The technique served as a minimal proof of concept for a theory, proposed by the neuroscientist Karl Friston, that self-organizing biological systems tend to minimize surprise whenever possible. By showing that neurons will reorganize themselves to avoid chaotic stimulus, Cortical Labs demonstrated one possible approach for programming living matter. But the experiment also signaled that the CL-1 could be considered hardware for testing theories of cognition. “Not to try and make our stuff sound so grandiose,” Kagan told me, “but I would say the CL-1 is to theoretical neuroscience as the Large Hadron Collider was to theoretical physics.”Kagan, to be fair, enjoys a grandiose claim. In the Pong paper, he and his colleagues claimed that the neurons, “embodied” within the game, displayed a form of sentience. Many in the research community balked at this cavalier use of language; one particularly polemic response, published in the journal Neuron, accused Cortical Labs of “hijacking” the very concept of sentience.But as Alon Loeffler, a scientist at Cortical Labs, later explained to me, our brains are embedded in an environment, and responding to that environment in real time is what brains do—it’s what brains are for. Since neurons in a dish don’t benefit from those constant feedback loops of action and experience, the game fills the gap. “A game is just a version of the world,” Loeffler said.“The world’s first code-deployable biological computer,” says Cortical Labs.Cortical Labs is aiming to become the Nvidia of neural computing.The Pong program comes preinstalled on the Cortical Cloud, as a package of easily deployable Python code. When I ran the Australian neurons through a two-hour session, I watched as they incrementally improved their game in real time. In the end, their longest rally was 10 accurate shots, which beats my tennis game handily. It was impressive, but now the neurons are leveling up.For one, they have learned to play Doom.When I set out to report this story, I was sure it was about consciousness: the eerie moment a quarter-peanut of flesh sparks with self-knowledge, and what that precipice means for the researchers responsible. I imagined long dark nights of the cell and tiny funerals for spent neurons. What I found, however, was that nearly all scientists who keep organoids see the consciousness question as a distraction.Most bristle when asked. They gesture to the organoids themselves—tiny balls bobbing in liquid solution like droplets of olive oil in vinegar—as if to say, give me a break. “Consciousness is so qualitative,” complained Annie Kathuria, an organoid researcher, when I visited her lab at Johns Hopkins. “How am I supposed to measure something qualitative on a tissue that’s floating in a dish? Someone has to define it. That’s what I say to everyone: Define to me what consciousness is, in quantitative terms.”The request is rhetorical, of course. Humans have been trying to define consciousness since the days of Plato and nobody’s come close to nailing down the general idea, let alone a list of quantitative metrics. But it reflects a strong tendency in biology labs to want to focus on the practical, rather than the philosophical. When I spoke to Kathuria, she sipped from a Venti Starbucks tea and regularly glanced at the whiteboard over my shoulder, covered in a list of dozens of drug screenings her lab was on the hook for. Defining the nature of mind was the last thing on her mind.That’s a job for the philosophers. Publishing papers about the edge cases of sentience has become something of a cottage industry in contemporary philosophy. Do zombies have moral status? Should robots have rights? What is it like to be a bat? Is an organoid sentient? Opinions vary. The philosopher Tim Bayne worries that organoids, isolated in their petri dishes, could become “islands of awareness.” Jonathan Birch, a professor of philosophy at the London School of Economics, thinks we’re in trouble if organoids ever grow a brain stem, which he argues functions as a “power cable” for consciousness.Others suggest thresholds based on the number of neurons, or organoid size. But thresholds are difficult to quantify too. “You cannot draw a barrier that will hold based on a number,” explained John Evans, the sociologist at UCSD. “You could say ‘you can’t grow anything larger than 4 millimeters.’ Well, how about 5 millimeters? There’s no morally relevant distinction between the two.”Conveniently, organoids can’t grow much bigger than 5 millimeters anyway. Once they reach a certain size, without a vascular system to pump in oxygen and pump out metabolic wastes, they develop a “necrotic core” and suffocate. This has created an upper ceiling for the organoid debate, but it won’t hold much longer. At Johns Hopkins, the nanotechnologist David Gracias is developing biomimetic artificial arteries; across town, at the Medical School, Kathuria creates rough blood vessel networks from endothelial organoids. Researchers are keeping organoids alive longer and longer. Muotri’s record, of three years, might’ve gone longer had someone in his lab not dropped the dish.“The goal is to get to a 1-centimeter brain organoid,” said Thomas Hartung, as he walked me around the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing, or CAAT, at Johns Hopkins, where he’s experimenting with new perfusion systems to get around the bloodlessness problem. One centimeter is roughly the size of a mouse brain—“a completely different beast,” Hartung said, than the 500-micrometer organoids he’s accustomed to.Hartung, a German-born toxicologist, has been working with organoids for over a decade. He’s the picture of a genial scientist. When we met, he sported an oversized cardigan and a beaded necklace made by his 9-year-old daughter. His wife, Lena Smirnova, is a neurotoxicologist and runs a lab at CAAT. Where Hartung is bearish and avuncular, with the loping Teutonic accent of a laid-back Werner Herzog, Smirnova is petite, with a bowl cut and a punctilious manner. The odd coupling seems to work for them. When I asked Smirnova if she’d ever make an organoid out of her own cells, she laughed so abruptly it sounded like she barked. “This is actually something between the two of us,” Hartung said, sheepishly. He’d offered her some of his stem cells, as an act of love, and she has so far refused to do anything with them.Hartung and Smirnova are leading figures in organoid research and have been vocal public supporters of the idea that organoids will revolutionize computing. In 2023, after organizing an international scholarly community, they published a splashy “Declaration” for a field they christened “organoid intelligence,” or OI. During my visit, however, the organoids in the CAAT lab weren’t doing much computing. They were mostly being dosed with heavy metals. OI is a buzzy idea, and it has drawn a lot of media attention. But practically, it’s a long-term goal. For now, organoids remain what they have always been—glorified lab rats.Nearly every organoid researcher I met reporting this piece told me the same fact: that in human clinical trials, the failure rate for neuropsychiatric drugs is close to 95 percent. The pipeline for new medications for conditions like depression, Alzheimer’s, and epilepsy is long, and often dry. That’s because drugs are ordinarily tested on animals, not people, and animal testing has never been the most physiologically relevant way to ensure the efficacy of drugs—it’s just been the most practical one. Organoids have changed that calculus.“Think about nonhuman primates, which is the model closest to us—these monkeys with electrodes in their heads,” Hartung said. “At best, you have a battery of five, six monkeys sitting there and doing their experiments. We’re producing, in one six-well plate, up to 4,000 brain organoids.” In this context, OI isn’t an end as much as it is a means. An organoid trained to play Pong, for example, is a perfect test subject to study how drugs affect learning and memory.In his office, Hartung showed me a simple video game his team is working on—a platformer with varying obstacles for the brain organoids to “jump” over. The idea is to train the organoids to respond to electrical signals representing those obstacles. Once they’ve learned this task, Hartung can ask questions like: How long do brain organoids remember when to “jump”? What effect do Alzheimer’s drugs have on the strength and duration of those memories?Underneath his desk, Hartung keeps a cardboard box filled with bottles of red wine, which he suggested we crack open twice before I left. He believes all the best conversations happen after 5 pm, and he paid for his graduate studies, back in Germany, doing stand-up comedy (he compares his comedic style to Bill Maher’s). The years of gigging gave him a head for PR.Organoid intelligence is, above all, good PR—a savvily branded attractor for funding and talent in a wide-open field. “I think the pie is too big for anybody to eat,” he said, leaning back in his chair. “What is really important is to tell the people about the opportunity of the pie so that we jointly have a feast. I will try as quickly as possible to eat my piece, which is the use for this in drug development, or in identifying substances which are impacting brain diseases. That’s my business.”Business is booming. In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health announced that it will no longer award grant funding to research that relies exclusively on animal testing, encouraging consideration of “new approach models,” like organoids, instead; in September, the NIH announced an $87 million investment in building a Standardized Organoid Modeling Center. Fortunately for the NIH, since organoids are made with induced pluripotent stem cells from consenting adult donors, they don’t inspire the same religious ire as embryonic stem cell research did in the 1990s. And unlike lab rats or primates, organoid testing doesn’t irk the animal rights crowd.Recent studies suggest that ordinary people, by and large, aren’t much bothered by organoids. When they do lodge an objection, it’s not because globs of neural cells might someday achieve human-level sentience. It’s because brain organoids are creepy. They muddy the line between person and thing, which, like the difference between humans and animals, or between the dead and the living, is a fundamental distinction that transcends cultures.In 2017, a pair of neuroscientists at University College London took a small sample of skin cells from the science journalist Philip Ball’s arm and made them into a brain organoid. Eight months later, gazing at their creation under the microscope, Ball felt an “unsettling frisson” at the idea that this living tissue, formed from his flesh as Eve from Adam’s rib, pulsed with the same electrical signals that animated his own brain. Although their structure was comparatively primitive, the neurons in Ball’s organoid were nonetheless communicating with one another. “These are not ‘thoughts,’” he told himself. “But they are what thoughts are made from.”Cajoled into becoming a mini-brain, Ball’s cells shifted ontological categories. Nobody could deny they were still alive, but it wasn’t Ball’s life they were living anymore. As Ball observes in his book How to Grow a Human, life is supposed to be a one-way journey: Sperm fertilizes egg, egg becomes zygote, and from this single cell cleave the trillions of facets that make us. This “seems conceptually unproblematic, so long as we can regard it all along as a coherent, boundaried organism with a unique history,” Ball writes. “But if you can take a tiny part of that mass of cells, rewind the tape and make a fresh start, then this unity starts to dissolve.” Kept warm and well fed in a petri dish, our cells carry on quite happily without us. Are they still ours?Microphotographs of wired-up neural cultures.Somewhere between the few million neurons in a brain organoid and the billions more that make up our minds, selfhood emerges—and absolutely nobody knows when. It reminds me of something the gnomic science-fiction writer Ted Chiang observed in a 2021 interview. “Suffering precedes moral agency in the developmental ladder,” he said. “In the process of developing machines that are conscious and moral agents, we will be inevitably creating billions of entities that are capable of suffering. And we will inevitably inflict suffering on them.”Chiang was talking about AI, but his point stands. After all, as digital interfaces between neural wetware and silicon hardware improve, we’ll have a harder time differentiating between the two, and it’s reasonable to imagine that efforts to engineer and standardize biological intelligence will inform the design of future AI systems. But what struck me, as I visited one cell culture lab after another, is the way their values inverted, rather than mimicked, those of the AI business.For the AI people, machine intelligence seems achievable, even inevitable. They “feel the AGI.” Part of this is hype; part of it is a willingness to take intelligence for what it does, as opposed to what it is. “If it quacks like a duck, it is a duck,” said John Evans, the UCSD sociologist. “The Silicon Valley types are super pragmatic. If AI is capable of doing what a human with consciousness does, they’ll call it consciousness.”Biologists who work with neural cultures, however, are far less likely to use such a word without plenty of agonizing caveats. These biologists cultivate the raw meat of mind every day; they’re in the privileged position to understand how colossally complex it really is. As biology and AI converge, the culture shock between these worldviews is likely to be bracing.For now, it seems that in the race toward conscious machines, there will be two lanes. One will be paved with rare earth minerals and silicon—forced, at enormous financial and energy cost, to model the brain from the top-down, in the form of artificial neural networks. Although there’s a lot these systems can do well, they will never be brains. Nothing forged from silicon ever could. As Cortical Labs’ Brett Kagan put it, “How can you have a truly adaptable, flexible system in an inflexible substrate?”Which leaves the other path. Admittedly, this one will be slippery and meandering—adapting, as all living things do, to the journey as it goes. It might not be the most direct route, but in the evolutionary history of life on Earth, it’s the only thing that has ever led to intelligence.So I’m betting on the neurons. I made up my mind back at that strange mothership of a library in San Diego, when I saw those axons reaching for one another across the void. Something in the innocence of their striving moved me. After all, my cells and yours have been doing the same thing since the day we were born. Trying to connect. And one thing we can count on—through the rise and fall of silicon—is that they’re never going to stop.What Say You?Let us know what you think about this article in the comments below. blocks.html_en: In cell culture labs around the world, human brain organoids live out their short lives as neural guinea pigs, testing the effects of diseases, toxins, and new pharmaceuticals. But they may soon be on to more glamorous pursuits. At the University of San Diego, organoids are guiding spidery robots through mazes and taking hero doses of psychedelics. At Johns Hopkins, they’re forming the basis of novel biocomputing systems. And at a startup in Melbourne, they’re playing video games like Pong and Doom.

While the rest of us are distracted by large language models and AI agents, they’re going straight to the source of intelligence, cultivating living neurons and teaching themselves to program them with electrical signals and hits of dopamine. In the future, they wager, artificial intelligence won’t be artificial at all. It’ll be built from the stuff of life itself.

blocks.html_en: The most metal building at UC San Diego is the library. An inverted concrete ziggurat, the Geisel Library—named for the children’s author better known as Dr. Seuss—looms over an otherwise bucolic campus on spindly, two-story legs. On a recent afternoon, as a marine layer hung low in the eucalyptus groves, it looked particularly like the mothership of a brutalist alien race.

It depicted a clump of human brain cells, silhouetted in black against the milky white of a petri dish. A corona of axons, the threadlike nerve endings that transmit electrical impulses across the brain, stretched outward from the clump with palpable yearning.

blocks.html_en: Muotri is dashing, with a surfer’s tan and the aquiline profile of a figure on an ancient Roman coin. Over the past decade, his lab has dramatically expanded the scope of brain organoid research. He and his colleagues have revived genetic material from the hominin fossil record to create “Neanderthalized” brain organoids. They have sent organoid payloads to the International Space Station to study what cosmic radiation does to astronaut brains. But the issue closest to Muotri’s heart is autism. His 18-year-old son is autistic and receives 24-hour care. By studying brain organoids grown from the cells of autistic donors—including his son—he hopes to pinpoint where the neural development of autistic children differs from their neurotypical counterparts.

blocks.html_en: It’s 3:30 pm in Los Angeles, which means it’s tomorrow morning in Australia. I’m sitting on the fire escape of my office building, peering at a grid of 59 squares on my laptop screen. I’ve been told that each of the squares represents an electrode in the Melbourne laboratory of the biocomputing startup Cortical Labs. And on each of those electrodes is a tiny culture of living human neurons. At the moment, my screen is registering fleeting spikes from those neurons—the spontaneous activity of brain matter in a vacuum. I click a square, zapping off an electrical hello to neurons 8,000 miles away. In response, all 59 electrodes spike at once.

blocks.html_en: But that’s the reality of the Cortical Cloud. Each is the size of an elongated toaster and boasts an onboard life-support system capable of keeping a culture of up to a million neurons alive for six months. With the CL-1, Cortical Labs is aiming to become the Nvidia of neural computing, providing hardware and, let’s say, “neurons as a service” with a sub-millisecond delay.

blocks.html_en: Kagan is a new father; as we spoke, his toddler ran riot in the background. But he’s no stranger to young and unruly forms of intelligence. In 2022, using a system similar to what currently powers the Cortical Cloud, Kagan grew a neural culture on a microchip and trained it to play the 1972 Atari game Pong, rewarding the neurons with predictable electrical pulses when they made correct decisions and punishing them with chaotic bursts when they made mistakes.

blocks.html_en: The technique served as a minimal proof of concept for a theory, proposed by the neuroscientist Karl Friston, that self-organizing biological systems tend to minimize surprise whenever possible. By showing that neurons will reorganize themselves to avoid chaotic stimulus, Cortical Labs demonstrated one possible approach for programming living matter. But the experiment also signaled that the CL-1 could be considered hardware for testing theories of cognition. “Not to try and make our stuff sound so grandiose,” Kagan told me, “but I would say the CL-1 is to theoretical neuroscience as the Large Hadron Collider was to theoretical physics.”

blocks.html_en: Hartung, a German-born toxicologist, has been working with organoids for over a decade. He’s the picture of a genial scientist. When we met, he sported an oversized cardigan and a beaded necklace made by his 9-year-old daughter. His wife, Lena Smirnova, is a neurotoxicologist and runs a lab at CAAT. Where Hartung is bearish and avuncular, with the loping Teutonic accent of a laid-back Werner Herzog, Smirnova is petite, with a bowl cut and a punctilious manner. The odd coupling seems to work for them. When I asked Smirnova if she’d ever make an organoid out of her own cells, she laughed so abruptly it sounded like she barked. “This is actually something between the two of us,” Hartung said, sheepishly. He’d offered her some of his stem cells, as an act of love, and she has so far refused to do anything with them.

blocks.html_en: Hartung and Smirnova are leading figures in organoid research and have been vocal public supporters of the idea that organoids will revolutionize computing. blocks.html_en: Nearly every organoid researcher I met reporting this piece told me the same fact: that in human clinical trials, the failure rate for neuropsychiatric drugs is close to 95 percent. The pipeline for new medications for conditions like depression, Alzheimer’s, and epilepsy is long, and often dry. That’s because drugs are ordinarily tested on animals, not people, and animal testing has never been the most physiologically relevant way to ensure the efficacy of drugs—it’s just been the most practical one. Organoids have changed that calculus.

blocks.html_en: Business is booming. In July 2025, the National Institutes of Health announced that it will no longer award grant funding to research that relies exclusively on animal testing, encouraging consideration of “new approach models,” like organoids, instead; in September, the NIH announced an $87 million investment in building a Standardized Organoid Modeling Center. Fortunately for the NIH, since organoids are made with induced pluripotent stem cells from consenting adult donors, they don’t inspire the same religious ire as embryonic stem cell research did in the 1990s. blocks.html_en: In 2017, a pair of neuroscientists at University College London took a small sample of skin cells from the science journalist Philip Ball’s arm and made them into a brain organoid. Eight months later, gazing at their creation under the microscope, Ball felt an “unsettling frisson” at the idea that this living tissue, formed from his flesh as Eve from Adam’s rib, pulsed with the same electrical signals that animated his own brain. Although their structure was comparatively primitive, the neurons in Ball’s organoid were nonetheless communicating with one another. “These are not ‘thoughts,’” he told himself. “But they are what thoughts are made from.”

blocks.html_en: Cajoled into becoming a mini-brain, Ball’s cells shifted ontological categories. Nobody could deny they were still alive, but it wasn’t Ball’s life they were living anymore. As Ball observes in his book How to Grow a Human, life is supposed to be a one-way journey: Sperm fertilizes egg, egg becomes zygote, and from this single cell cleave the trillions of facets that make us. This “seems conceptually unproblematic, so long as we can regard it all along as a coherent, boundaried organism with a unique history,” Ball writes. “But if you can take a tiny part of that mass of cells, rewind the tape and make a fresh start, then this unity starts to dissolve.” Kept warm and well fed in a petri dish, our cells carry on quite happily without us. It reminds me of something the gnomic science-fiction writer Ted Chiang observed in a 2021 interview. “Suffering precedes moral agency in the developmental ladder,” he said. “In the process of developing machines that are conscious and moral agents, we will be inevitably creating billions of entities that are capable of suffering. content_html_zh:
我要告诉你一个秘密。 您体内的每个细胞都有变得更聪明的潜力。 我的意思并不是隐喻，也不是“身体记录分数”之类的意思。 我的意思是，如果实验室里的生物学家采集你的皮肤样本并非常仔细地操纵其中的细胞，他们实际上可以制造出大脑。 他们一直这样做。

当然，它不是像眼睛后面那样复杂的大脑，而是一团灰质，具有数百万个可以发送和接收电信号的神经元。 生物学家将这些奇怪的创造物称为人类大脑类器官。 在子宫般的 98.6 华氏度下保持八个月，它们会产生重复的振荡（脑电波），与早产儿产生的振荡几乎没有区别。

在世界各地的细胞培养实验室中，人脑类器官作为神经豚鼠度过了短暂的生命，测试疾病、毒素和新药物的影响。 但他们可能很快就会追求更迷人的追求。 在圣地亚哥大学，类器官正在引导蜘蛛机器人穿过迷宫并服用英雄剂量的迷幻药。 在约翰·霍普金斯大学，他们正在构建新型生物计算系统的基础。 在墨尔本的一家初创公司，他们正在玩 Pong 和 Doom 等电子游戏。

生物学家做了最可怕的事情。 当我们其他人被大型语言模型和人工智能代理分散注意力时，他们直接走向智能的源头，培养活的神经元，并教自己用电信号和多巴胺的刺激来对它们进行编程。 他们打赌，未来人工智能将不再是人工的。 它将由生活本身的材料构建而成。

加州大学圣地亚哥分校最金属的建筑是图书馆。 盖泽尔图书馆是一座倒置的混凝土金字形神塔，以儿童作家苏斯博士的名字命名，它以细长的两层楼腿矗立在原本充满田园气息的校园之上。 最近的一个下午，当一层海洋层低垂在桉树林中时，它看起来特别像一个野蛮的外星种族的母舰。

那天，盖泽尔大学下沉式的大厅挂满了该大学收藏的科学图片。 在折叠蛋白质的 CGI 渲染和底栖海洋生物的宏观照片中，一张图像脱颖而出。 它描绘了一群人类脑细胞，在培养皿的乳白色衬托下呈现出黑色的轮廓。 轴突的冠状，即在大脑中传递电脉冲的线状神经末梢，带着明显的渴望从轴突向外延伸。

无论是在我们的头骨中还是在培养皿中，神经元只想找到彼此，并跨越空虚，形成突触，突触的电颤动构成了思维的基础。 他们非常擅长。 如果你把松散的脑细胞放在一起，它们就会繁殖并相互连接，直到凝聚成自主的组织球。 人脑类器官实际上可以自己制造。

距离 Geisel 步行 20 分钟的加州大学圣地亚哥分校桑福德干细胞研究所 (Sanford Stem Cell Institute) 已有数以万计的人。 “无论你把它们放在什么环境中，它们做的第一件事就是尝试建立联系，”巴西发育生物学家阿利森·穆特里（Alysson Muotri）说道，当时我们凝视着他办公室窗外太平洋的蓝色平面。 “与培养皿连接，与电极连接，相互连接。 这是我们大脑的固有属性，即连接。”

穆特里很潇洒，有着冲浪者的晒黑皮肤和古罗马硬币上人物的鹰隼轮廓。 在过去的十年中，他的实验室极大地扩大了大脑类器官的研究范围。 他和他的同事们从古人类化石记录中恢复了遗传物质，以创造出“尼安德特人化”的大脑类器官。 他们已将类器官有效载荷发送到国际空间站，以研究宇宙辐射对宇航员大脑的影响。 但穆特里最关心的问题是自闭症。 他18岁的儿子患有自闭症，接受24小时护理。 通过研究从自闭症捐献者（包括他的儿子）的细胞中培育出的大脑类器官，他希望查明自闭症儿童的神经发育与神经正常儿童的不同之处。

这不是侵入性手术。 要制作大脑类器官，您所需要的只是我之前提到的皮肤样本。 （血液、头发或牙齿样本也可以。） 你将成体细胞引入一些特殊的蛋白质中，将它们恢复到胚胎状态。 如果有第二次成熟的机会，这些所谓的诱导多能干细胞可以变成任何东西：会哭泣的泪腺类器官、会跳动的心脏类器官、或...... 好吧，这就是问题所在。

正如一位生物伦理学家告诉我的那样，子宫内大脑的发育是科学知识的“黑匣子”。 从历史上看，我们对它的了解很多都是从小鼠研究中推断出来的。 但有了类器官，干细胞转化为神经元再转化为脑组织的过程就在众目睽睽之下发生。 理论上，有一天，科学家们可以研究一群正在分裂的细胞如何聚集在一起创造出一种思维——例如，用 860 亿个神经元创造出一个名叫 Alysson Muotri 的人。

或者另一位名叫克莱尔·L. 埃文斯此刻正靠在穆特里的肩膀上，目瞪口呆地看着显微镜下一盘漂浮的大脑。 从视觉上看，类器官并不引人注目。它们是不透明的、鼻涕色的，大小和形状与奇亚籽相似。 Muotri 的类器官含有 500 万个细胞，其中 250 万个是神经元。 （其余的是非神经胶质细胞，充当支架。） 他向我保证，这相当于蜜蜂大脑的大小。 我怀疑这是他缓和我可能存在的道德问题的方式。 尽管昆虫有感知能力的证据越来越多，但无脊椎动物研究仍然不受联邦动物福利法的约束。 正如社会学家、加州大学圣地亚哥分校实践伦理研究所联席主任约翰·埃文斯（John Evans）在我漫步到他的办公室寻求人文主义观点时对我所说的那样，“你不需要获得许可就可以折磨尽可能多的苍蝇。”

目前，你也不需要获得许可来折磨大脑类器官。 从生物伦理学的角度来看，他们不是人，而是人。他们甚至不是动物。 如果有一天类器官从蜜蜂大小变成了小鼠大小，那么这个协议就必须进化。 问题是，没有人知道在哪里划清界限。 感知力并不是一个固定的概念。甚至不清楚在没有身体或对世界的感官体验的情况下你是否能够拥有知觉。 忘记称类器官为有意识吧。 “想象一下，你的一生都在玻璃管里度过——你能想象你所拥有的意识吗？” 埃文斯问我。 “心灵哲学家会告诉你，如果没有经验，我们所谓的意识是不可能的。” 他补充道，为了制造出有意识的类器官，“你首先必须让类器官拥有经验。”

这并非不可能。 我们都看过《黑客帝国》。 对于大脑来说，整个生命的摩天轮只是化学和电流的脉冲声。 为了给类器官一种“体验”，穆特里所要做的就是从羊膜粘液中取出一个类器官，将其放在导电的石墨烯片上，然后——不要在它上面放得太细——将其击碎。

类器官喜欢被电击吗？ 穆特里不确定。 他所知道的是，它们会对电信号做出反应，记住它们，并最终预测它们。 对他来说，这证明它们正在成熟，成为人类发展更有用的模型。 但对于其他研究人员来说，这种电通信完全代表着另一回事：生命物质，就像计算机一样，是可编程的。 这就是事情变得真正奇怪的地方。

现在是洛杉矶下午 3:30，这意味着澳大利亚是明天早上。 我坐在办公楼的防火梯上，凝视着笔记本电脑屏幕上由 59 个方格组成的网格。 有人告诉我，每个方块代表生物计算初创公司 Cortical Labs 墨尔本实验室的一个电极。 每个电极上都有一个微小的活体人类神经元培养物。 目前，我的屏幕正在记录这些神经元的短暂尖峰——真空中大脑物质的自发活动。 我点击一个方块，向 8,000 英里外的神经元发出电击问候。 作为响应，所有 59 个电极同时出现峰值。

有一瞬间，我因一种新的力量而感到头晕。 我四处点击，让那些远处的神经元跳跃；我的屏幕上充满了电脉冲的波峰和波谷。 我翻页查看神经元的环境设置。 如果我愿意，我可以降低他们的机上温度或用核武器摧毁他们精确的氧气和二氧化碳气体混合物。 如果我这么做的话，他们肯定会死。 这是我能想象到的计算领域的一次重大范式转变：无论你把代码搞得多么糟糕，计算机上的东西在现实生活中通常都不会消失。

但这就是皮质云的现实。 在墨尔本，Cortical Labs 培养扁平神经培养物（干细胞由公司创始人捐赠）并将其加载到名为 CL-1 的时尚白色生物“计算机”中。 每个都有一个细长的烤面包机大小，并拥有一个机载生命支持系统，能够使多达一百万个神经元的培养物存活六个月。 Cortical Labs 的目标是通过 CL-1 成为神经计算领域的 Nvidia，提供硬件以及延迟亚毫秒级的“神经元即服务”。

目前，这些神经计算机最感兴趣的是那些想要研究神经元而不需要自己承担繁琐的实验室管理工作的研究人员。 然而，最终该公司希望神经元能够证明自己是一种节能、有弹性的基础，适用于更通用的计算应用——包括目前由人工智能处理的一些任务，如图像识别和分类。

当我通过 Zoom 联系 Cortical Labs 首席运营官布雷特·卡根 (Brett Kagan) 时，他说：“当你思考你想从人工智能中得到什么时，它就是生物学。” “你希望它尽可能地自我修复。 你希望它具有适应性。 你希望它长久存在。 您希望它节能。 这些都是你在生物学中免费获得的功能。”

卡根是一位新父亲；当我们说话时，他的孩子在后台骚乱。 但他对年轻且不守规矩的智力形式并不陌生。 2022 年，卡根使用类似于目前为皮质云提供动力的系统，在微芯片上培养了一种神经培养物，并训练它玩 1972 年的 Atari 游戏 Pong，当神经元做出正确的决定时，用可预测的电脉冲奖励它们，当它们犯错时，用混乱的脉冲来惩罚它们。

该技术是神经科学家卡尔·弗里斯顿（Karl Friston）提出的理论的最小概念证明，即自组织生物系统倾向于尽可能减少意外。 通过证明神经元会自我重组以避免混乱的刺激，皮质实验室展示了一种对生命物质进行编程的可能方法。 但该实验也表明 CL-1 可以被视为测试认知理论的硬件。 “并不是想让我们的东西听起来如此宏大，”卡根告诉我，“但我想说 CL-1 对于理论神经科学来说就像大型强子对撞机对于理论物理学一样。”

公平地说，卡根的主张很宏大。 在 Pong 论文中，他和他的同事声称，游戏中“体现”的神经元表现出某种形式的感知能力。 研究界的许多人对这种漫不经心的语言使用感到犹豫。 《神经元》杂志上发表了一篇特别引起争议的回应，指责皮质实验室“劫持”了感知的概念。

但正如皮质实验室的科学家阿隆·洛夫勒后来向我解释的那样，我们的大脑嵌入在一个环境中，实时响应该环境就是大脑的作用——这就是大脑的用途。 由于培养皿中的神经元无法从动作和经验的持续反馈循环中受益，因此游戏填补了这一空白。 “游戏只是世界的一个版本，”洛夫勒说。

Pong 程序作为易于部署的 Python 代码包预安装在 Cortical Cloud 上。 当我对澳大利亚神经元进行两个小时的训练时，我观察到他们实时地逐步改进了他们的游戏。 最后，他们最长的对打是10次准确击球，轻松击败了我的网球比赛。 这令人印象深刻，但现在神经元正在升级。

其一，他们学会了玩《毁灭战士》。

当我开始报道这个故事时，我确信它与意识有关：四分之一花生的肉因自我认识而火花的怪诞时刻，以及这个悬崖对于负责的研究人员意味着什么。 我想象着牢房里漫长的黑夜和为耗尽的神经元举行的小型葬礼。 然而，我发现，几乎所有保存类器官的科学家都认为意识问题是一种干扰。

当被问及时，大多数人都感到愤怒。 他们对类器官本身做出手势——在液体溶液中摆动的小球，就像醋中的橄榄油滴一样——仿佛在说，让我休息一下。 当我参观约翰·霍普金斯大学的类器官研究员安妮·卡图里亚 (Annie Kathuria) 的实验室时，她抱怨道：“意识是定性的。” “我该如何对漂浮在培养皿中的组织进行定性测量？ 必须有人来定义它。 这就是我对每个人说的：从数量上给我定义什么是意识。”

当然，这个要求只是口头上的。 自柏拉图时代以来，人类一直在尝试定义意识，但没有人能够确定总体概念，更不用说一系列定量指标了。 但这反映了生物学实验室想要关注实践而不是哲学的强烈趋势。 当我与卡图里亚交谈时，她喝了一杯 Venti 星巴克茶，并定期扫视我肩后的白板，上面列出了她的实验室正在进行的数十项药物筛查。 定义心性是她最不关心的事情。

这是哲学家的工作。 发表关于感知边缘案例的论文已经成为当代哲学中的家庭手工业。 僵尸有道德地位吗？ 机器人应该有权利吗？ 成为一只蝙蝠是什么感觉？ 类器官有感知能力吗？ 意见不一。 哲学家蒂姆·贝恩担心，孤立在培养皿中的类器官可能会成为“意识岛屿”。 伦敦经济学院哲学教授乔纳森·伯奇 (Jonathan Birch) 认为，如果类器官长出脑干，我们就会遇到麻烦，他认为脑干的功能相当于意识的“电缆”。

其他人则根据神经元数量或类器官大小提出阈值。 但阈值也很难量化。 加州大学圣地亚哥分校的社会学家约翰·埃文斯解释说：“你无法根据数字来划定一个有效的障碍。” “你可以说‘你不能种植任何大于 4 毫米的东西。’ 那么，5毫米怎么样？ 两者之间没有道德上的区别。”

方便的是，类器官无论如何都不能长到超过 5 毫米。 一旦它们达到一定的大小，如果没有血管系统来泵入氧气和排出代谢废物，它们就会形成“坏死核心”并窒息而死。 这为类器官争论创造了一个上限，但它不会持续太久。 在约翰·霍普金斯大学，纳米技术专家 David Gracias 正在开发仿生人工动脉。在城镇另一边的医学院，卡图里亚利用内皮类器官创建了粗糙的血管网络。 研究人员正在使类器官的存活时间越来越长。 穆特里保持了三年的记录，如果他实验室里的人没有把盘子掉下来的话，可能会保持更长的时间。

“我们的目标是获得 1 厘米的大脑类器官，”托马斯·哈同 (Thomas Hartung) 带着我参观约翰·霍普金斯大学动物试验替代中心 (CAAT) 时说道，他正在那里试验新的灌注系统，以解决无血问题。 一厘米大约相当于小鼠大脑的大小，哈通说，与他习惯的 500 微米类器官相比，“这是一种完全不同的动物”。

哈同是一位出生于德国的毒理学家，十多年来一直致力于类器官研究。 他就像一位和蔼可亲的科学家。 当我们见面时，他穿着一件超大号的羊毛衫，戴着一条由他 9 岁的女儿制作的串珠项链。 他的妻子莉娜·斯米尔诺娃 (Lena Smirnova) 是一名神经毒理学家，在 CAAT 经营着一个实验室。 哈同性格悲观、慈祥，带着悠闲的维尔纳·赫尔佐格那样大步流星的日耳曼口音，而斯米尔诺娃身材娇小，留着碗形发型，举止一丝不苟。 这种奇怪的耦合似乎对他们有用。 当我问斯米尔诺娃是否会用自己的细胞制造类器官时，她笑得很突然，听起来就像在吠叫。 “这实际上是我们两个人之间的事情，”哈同不好意思地说。 作为一种爱的表现，他向她提供了一些干细胞，但她迄今为止拒绝对它们做任何事情。

哈同和斯米尔诺娃是类器官研究领域的领军人物，并且一直是类器官将彻底改变计算这一理念的公开支持者。 2023 年，在组织了一个国际学术团体后，他们为一个他们称之为“类器官智能”（OI）的领域发表了一份引人注目的“宣言”。 然而，在我访问期间，CAAT 实验室的类器官并没有进行太多计算。 他们大多服用了重金属。 OI 是一个很热门的想法，它引起了很多媒体的关注。 但实际上，这是一个长期目标。 目前，类器官仍然是它们原来的样子——美化的实验室老鼠。

我遇到的几乎每一位报道这篇文章的类器官研究人员都告诉我同样的事实：在人体临床试验中，神经精神药物的失败率接近 95%。 治疗抑郁症、阿尔茨海默病和癫痫等疾病的新药研发渠道很长，而且往往很干燥。 这是因为药物通常是在动物身上进行测试，而不是在人身上进行测试，而动物测试从来都不是确保药物功效的最生理相关的方法——它只是最实用的一种方法。 类器官改变了这种计算方式。

“想想非人类灵长类动物，它们是最接近我们的模型——这些猴子的头上有电极，”哈通说。 “最好的情况是，有五六只猴子坐在那里做实验。 我们正在一个六孔板中生产多达 4,000 个脑类器官。” 在这种情况下，OI 与其说是目的，不如说是一种手段。 例如，经过训练打乒乓球的类器官是研究药物如何影响学习和记忆的完美测试对象。

在他的办公室里，哈同向我展示了他的团队正在开发的一款简单的视频游戏——一款平台游戏，其中有不同的障碍可供大脑类器官“跳过”。 这个想法是训练类器官对代表这些障碍的电信号做出反应。 一旦学会了这项任务，哈通就可以提出这样的问题：大脑类器官能记住何时“跳跃”多久？ 阿尔茨海默病药物对这些记忆的强度和持续时间有什么影响？

哈同在他的办公桌下放了一个纸板箱，里面装满了红酒瓶，他建议我们在离开之前将其打开两次。 他相信所有最好的对话都发生在下午 5 点之后，他支付了研究生学费，回到德国，做单口喜剧（他将自己的喜剧风格与比尔·马赫的喜剧风格进行了比较）。 多年的演出经历让他具备了公关头脑。

最重要的是，类器官智能是良好的公关——在广阔的领域中吸引资金和人才的精明品牌吸引器。 “我认为这个馅饼太大了，任何人都吃不完，”他靠在椅子上说道。 “真正重要的是告诉人们馅饼的机会，以便我们共同享受一顿盛宴。 我会尽快尝试吃掉我的作品，这将用于药物开发或识别影响脑部疾病的物质。 这是我的事。”

生意兴隆。 2025 年 7 月，美国国立卫生研究院宣布将不再向完全依赖动物测试的研究提供资助，而是鼓励考虑类器官等“新方法模型”； 9 月，NIH 宣布投资 8700 万美元建设标准化类器官建模中心。 对于 NIH 来说幸运的是，由于类器官是用来自同意的成年捐赠者的诱导多能干细胞制成的，因此它们不会像 20 世纪 90 年代的胚胎干细胞研究那样激起宗教愤怒。 与实验室老鼠或灵长类动物不同，类器官测试不会激怒动物权利群体。

最近的研究表明，总的来说，普通人并不太受类器官的困扰。 当他们确实提出反对意见时，并不是因为神经细胞团有一天可能会获得人类水平的感知能力。 这是因为大脑类器官令人毛骨悚然。 它们混淆了人与物之间的界限，就像人类与动物之间、死者与生者之间的区别一样，这是超越文化的根本区别。

2017年，伦敦大学学院的两位神经科学家从科学记者菲利普·鲍尔的手臂上采集了一小部分皮肤细胞样本，并将其制成了大脑类器官。 八个月后，鲍尔在显微镜下凝视着它们的创造物，一想到这个活体组织，就像夏娃从亚当的肋骨中形成一样，由他的肉体形成，发出的电信号与激活他自己大脑的电信号相同，他感到一种“令人不安的颤抖”。 尽管它们的结构相对原始，但鲍尔类器官中的神经元仍然可以相互通信。 “这些不是‘想法’，”他告诉自己。 “但思想就是由它们构成的。”

在诱骗下，鲍尔的细胞变成了一个迷你大脑，改变了本体论的范畴。 没有人可以否认他们还活着，但他们已经不再是鲍尔的生活了。 正如鲍尔在他的《如何培育人类》一书中所观察到的那样，生命应该是一场单程旅程：精子使卵子受精，卵子成为受精卵，然后从这个单细胞分裂出数万亿个面，从而构成了我们。 鲍尔写道，这“在概念上似乎没有问题，只要我们一直将其视为一个具有独特历史的连贯的、有边界的有机体”。 “但如果你能从大量细胞中取出一小部分，倒带并重新开始，那么这种团结就会开始瓦解。” 在培养皿中保持温暖且营养充足，我们的细胞在没有我们的情况下也能快乐地生存。 他们还是我们的吗？

在大脑类器官的几百万个神经元和构成我们思想的数十亿个神经元之间的某个地方，自我出现了——而且绝对没有人知道何时出现。 这让我想起了格言科幻作家特德·姜 (Ted Jiang) 在 2021 年接受采访时观察到的事情。 “在发展阶梯上，苦难先于道德能动性，”他说。 “在开发有意识和道德的机器的过程中，我们将不可避免地创造出数十亿个能够承受痛苦的实体。 我们将不可避免地给他们带来痛苦。”

蒋谈论的是人工智能，但他的观点是正确的。 毕竟，随着神经湿件和硅硬件之间的数字接口的改进，我们将很难区分两者，并且可以合理地想象，生物智能的工程和标准化工作将为未来人工智能系统的设计提供信息。 但当我参观了一个又一个细胞培养实验室时，令我震惊的是，他们的价值观与人工智能行业的价值观相反，而不是模仿。

对于人工智能人来说，机器智能似乎是可以实现的，甚至是不可避免的。 他们“感受到了 AGI”。 其中一部分是炒作；其中一部分是愿意接受情报的用途，而不是情报本身。 “如果它像鸭子一样嘎嘎叫，那就是鸭子，”加州大学圣地亚哥分校社会学家约翰·埃文斯说。 “硅谷的人非常务实。 如果人工智能能够做有意识的人类所做的事情，他们就会称之为意识。”

然而，研究神经培养的生物学家在没有大量令人痛苦的警告的情况下不太可能使用这个词。 这些生物学家每天都在培育心灵的生肉；他们处于特权地位，能够理解它到底有多么复杂。 随着生物学和人工智能的融合，这些世界观之间的文化冲击可能会令人振奋。

目前看来，在朝向有意识机器的竞赛中，将有两条车道。 其中一个将用稀土矿物和硅铺成——被迫以巨大的财务和能源成本，以人工神经网络的形式自上而下地模拟大脑。 尽管这些系统可以做很多事情，但它们永远不会成为大脑。 硅锻造的任何东西都做不到这一点。 正如 Cortical Labs 的 Brett Kagan 所说，“如何在不灵活的基板上拥有真正适应性强的灵活系统？”

这就留下了另一条路。 诚然，这艘船将是湿滑而蜿蜒的——就像所有生物一样，适应它的旅程。 这可能不是最直接的途径，但在地球生命的进化史上，它是唯一通向智慧的途径。

所以我把赌注押在神经元上。 回到圣地亚哥那座奇怪的图书馆母舰时，当我看到那些轴突穿过虚空相互伸展时，我就下定了决心。 他们的纯真努力让我感动。 毕竟，从我们出生那天起，我的细胞和你的细胞就一直在做同样的事情。 正在尝试连接。 我们可以信赖的一件事是，通过硅的兴衰，它们永远不会停止。
